props.title: Oh, God! Book II

sections.content: Oh, God! Book II continues the divine comedy series with George Burns reprising his role as the Almighty, this time appearing to a young girl instead of John Denver's grocery store manager from Oh, God! (1977). The sequel marks a fascinating shift in how Hollywood approached faith-based comedy in the early 1980s, threading the needle between irreverent humor and sincere spiritual messaging. While the original film tackled adult skepticism, this follow-up explores childhood faith through Tracy Richards (Louanne), whose innocent belief contrasts sharply with her divorced parents' pragmatic worldview.

sections.content: The film sits within a unique period of Hollywood's relationship with religious themes. Unlike the reverent biblical epics of the 1950s like The Ten Commandments (1956) or the provocative religious horror of The Exorcist (1973), the Oh, God! series pioneered a gentler approach to faith-based storytelling. This middle-ground treatment influenced later works like Bruce Almighty (2003) and Evan Almighty (2007), which similarly balance comedy with spiritual messages. SUBHEAD: Impact on Family-Oriented Religious Cinema

Oh, God! Book II helped establish a template for family-friendly religious films that would flourish in later decades. Its influence can be seen in movies like Angels in the Outfield (1994) and Heaven Is for Real (2014), where children's spiritual experiences challenge adult skepticism. The film's handling of divorce through a spiritual lens also paved the way for movies like Mrs. Doubtfire (1993), which similarly uses fantastical elements to process family separation.
